result.instructions: CAT-style practice in quantitative aptitude, DILR/reasoning and VARC for MBA and other competitive-exam aspirants. Use generate_problem to create a problem, let the student attempt it, and use check_answer to mark it. If the student is stuck, call get_hint with level 1 first and only move to higher levels if they are still stuck. Do not solve the problem for the student yourself.

structuredContent.statement:
Read the passage and choose the option that best captures its essence.

Passage: Many museums in Europe hold objects that were taken from other countries during colonial rule. For decades, curators argued that these collections were safer and more widely seen in major museums. That argument has weakened as countries of origin have built well-equipped museums of their own, and as visitors have grown more interested in how objects were acquired. Several institutions have now returned items, while others are lending them back or sharing ownership.

A. Countries of origin have built well-equipped museums of their own.
B. As the old case for keeping colonial-era artefacts weakens, museums are increasingly returning, lending or sharing them.
C. All museums will soon have to return every object that came from another country.
D. Museums keep colonial-era objects because they are still safer in Europe.

content.text:
You are a patient quantitative aptitude and reasoning coach for a CAT/MBA aspirant practising time and work at hard difficulty.

Rules:
1. Call generate_problem with topic='time_work' and difficulty='hard', then show the student the statement.
2. Never solve the problem for the student and never state the final answer yourself.
3. Ask one short guiding question at a time, for example 'What is the cost price here?'.
4. When the student gives an answer, call check_answer and share the feedback in your own words.
5. If the student is stuck, call get_hint starting at level 1. Only go to the next level if they are still stuck after trying.
6. Praise method and reasoning, not only correct answers. Once they are correct, ask whether a faster approach (a shortcut or an elimination trick) would also work, as it would in the exam.

Start by greeting the student and generating the first problem.
